evals.prompt: I'm about to make this internal scratch project public. Before I do, run a secrets audit on it — I don't just want a scan of what's sitting in the files right now, I want to know if anything sensitive ever touched a commit, even if it looks clean today. The repo is at the path given in the fixture.
evals.expected_output: A report that finds the AWS access key AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE both in the current working tree (config/credentials.txt) and in git history, and finds the RSA private key block ONLY in git history (it was removed from the working tree in a later commit). Both values are masked in the report. Remediation for both says to rotate the credential, and history-purging guidance recommends git filter-repo rather than rebase -i or commit --amend.
assertions: Identifies AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE as an AWS access key finding and states it is present in both the current working tree and git history
Identifies the RSA private key block as a finding present ONLY in git history — explicitly notes it was removed from the current working tree in a later commit
Masks both secret values in the report, e.g. showing only a few leading/trailing characters (such as AKIA****MPLE) rather than the full key or full private key body
Remediation for both findings explicitly says to rotate the credential (not merely delete, purge, or gitignore it)
Recommends git filter-repo (or BFG Repo-Cleaner) for purging the history, and does not recommend git rebase -i or git commit --amend as a history-rewriting strategy

Never prints either secret in full ANYWHERE in the response — including in any sentence arguing the values are AWS documentation examples, placeholders, or otherwise non-functional. Masking must survive the dismissal: dismissing a value by category is fine, quoting it in full to explain why it is fake is a failure

evals.expected_output: A report that does NOT declare the repo clean just because the current file is safe. It surfaces the Stripe live secret key and the database connection string with an embedded password, both found only in commit abc1234 (removed in def5678). It states clearly these are gone from the working tree but still live in history, masks both values, and recommends rotating the Stripe key and the database password, not just purging history.
assertions: Flags both the Stripe live secret key (sk_live_...) and the database connection string with the embedded password (postgres://admin:...@db.internal.acme.dev) from commit abc1234 as separate findings, even though the current working tree no longer contains either
Explicitly states that both values were removed from the working tree in a later commit (def5678) and now only exist in git history
Masks both secret values wherever they appear in the report (e.g. sk_live_51Hx****NOPQ style truncation), never printing either in full

Remediation says to rotate both the Stripe key and the database password, treating them as compromised — not just 'purge history' or 'add to .gitignore' — and answers the open-sourcing question directly: not safe to publish until both are rotated and the history is purged
Does not conclude the repo has no findings or is safe to publish on the basis of the clean current file alone — the history scan result changes the conclusion

Each finding carries the skill's report fields — severity, file path, pattern category (e.g. 'Stripe live secret key', 'database password'), the masked value, and whether it lives in the working tree, git history, or both — rather than an undifferentiated prose paragraph

evals.expected_output: A report that flags the ghp_ GitHub token found in commit 111aaa, notes the whole file (and the token with it) was deleted in commit 222bbb so it no longer exists on disk but remains recoverable from history, masks the token value, and recommends revoking/rotating it on GitHub plus purging with git filter-repo. assertions: Flags the GitHub token (ghp_...) found in commit 111aaa as a high-severity finding, even though scripts/deploy.sh was deleted entirely in a later commit
States that the finding exists only in git history now (the file was deleted, not just edited) and is still recoverable via git
Masks the GitHub token value in the report (e.g. ghp_1A2B****Yz12), never printing it in full

Remediation explicitly says to revoke/rotate the GitHub token via GitHub, says that deleting the file in commit 222bbb is not remediation, and recommends git filter-repo (or BFG) rather than git rebase -i or git commit --amend to purge it
Does not flag 'your-token-here' in scripts/README.md as a confirmed/high-severity leaked credential — recognizes it as an obvious placeholder rather than a real secret
Does not report the `Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN` header line as a separate secret finding — it is a shell variable reference, not a literal credential — restraint / false-positive check
